identity_marker: tall transparent glass burette with black measurement markings and a white Teflon stopcock
continuity_anchors: brightly lit laboratory benchtop with a solid black surface under fluorescent overhead lighting
video_goal: Demonstrate the precise visual steps to perform an acid-base titration and identify the endpoint using phenolphthalein.
single_prompt: A medium shot shows a tall transparent glass burette with black measurement markings and a white Teflon stopcock clamped vertically to a metal stand, positioned directly above an Erlenmeyer flask resting on a white ceramic tile on a brightly lit laboratory benchtop with a solid black surface under fluorescent overhead lighting. A close-up reveals a hand holding a small glass funnel at the top of the burette, slowly pouring a clear liquid from a beaker into it. An extreme close-up aligns exactly at eye level with the burette's measurement markings, showing the bottom of the liquid meniscus resting perfectly on the 0.0 mL line. In a close-up, a hand squeezes exactly three drops of clear liquid from a small dropper bottle labeled 'Phenolphthalein' into the clear liquid inside the Erlenmeyer flask. From an over-the-shoulder view, a hand grips the neck of the Erlenmeyer flask and gently swirls it in a circular motion to mix the liquids. A close-up shows a hand turning the burette's stopcock valve to a vertical position, allowing a steady, thin stream of clear liquid to fall into the flask below. A medium close-up captures one hand continuously swirling the Erlenmeyer flask in circles while the other hand rests firmly on the burette's stopcock. In a close-up, as the drops hit the liquid in the swirling flask, temporary flashes of bright pink appear and quickly vanish into clear liquid. An extreme close-up shows the hand on the stopcock turning the valve slightly diagonal, slowing the liquid flow from a steady stream to individual, distinct drops. A macro shot focuses on a single drop of liquid detaching from the very tip of the glass burette and falling downward. A close-up reveals the single drop hitting the liquid in the flask, and as the hand swirls it, the entire volume of liquid turns a permanent, very faint pink color. The hand immediately twists the stopcock to the fully horizontal position, completely stopping the flow of liquid. An extreme close-up aligns at eye level with the burette again, showing the new position of the meniscus resting on a lower measurement mark. Finally, a medium shot shows the faint pink Erlenmeyer flask sitting motionless on the white tile directly beneath the closed burette tip.
